characters.name: Elimelech

genealogy.note: An Ephrathite of Bethlehemjudah (Ruth 1:2). No genealogy for Elimelech's own ancestry is given anywhere in Ruth.

verses.note: An Ephrathite of Bethlehemjudah, husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Chilion, who went to sojourn in Moab because of a famine in the land.
"And Elimelech Naomi's husband died; and she was left, and her two sons." He dies before any of the book's main action (chapters 2-4) takes place.
Naomi is described as one "that selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech's" — establishes the land later redeemed by Boaz as Elimelech's estate.

CORRECTION/HEDGE: Boaz's public declaration covers two adjoining but distinct customs. V.9 states he has bought "all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, of the hand of Naomi" (a joint family land-redemption). V.10, immediately following, ties the separate "raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" language specifically to Mahlon by name, as Ruth's husband — not to Elimelech. This entry does not attribute the name-raising language to Elimelech; see the mahlon entry for that clause. Whether "his inheritance" in v.10 means Mahlon's individual share or the combined family estate is not fully disambiguated by the text itself, and is not resolved as flat fact here.

funFacts: His name ("my God is king") is never commented on by the text itself — any thematic irony/fittingness read into it is an outside inference, not asserted here.
He dies off-page in Moab (Ruth 1:3) before the book's main action begins; every later scene revolves around the women and property he left behind.

characters.name: Naomi

genealogy.note: Wife of Elimelech, mother of Mahlon and Chilion (Ruth 1:2-5). Renamed herself "Mara" on returning to Bethlehem (Ruth 1:20-21). Legally/customarily framed as the one to whom Obed is "born" (Ruth 4:17) despite Ruth being his biological mother — see obed entry.

verses.note: Widowed by Elimelech's death, then loses both sons Mahlon and Chilion, left with her two daughters-in-law.
Urges Orpah and Ruth to return to their mothers' houses in Moab rather than follow her.
Returns to Bethlehem and tells the women there, "call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me."
Identifies Boaz as a kinsman of her husband's, later calling him "one of our next kinsmen."
Instructs Ruth to go to the threshing floor and approach Boaz.
The neighbor women bless her at Obed's birth; she takes the child, lays him in her bosom, and "became nurse unto it."

funFacts: Her name means "pleasant," which she explicitly contrasts with her chosen name "Mara" (bitter) in Ruth 1:20.
After chapter 1 she never again acts as directly as Ruth or Boaz do — her role shifts to counselor/planner (Ruth 3:1-4) and, at the end, caretaker of Obed (Ruth 4:16).

characters.name: Ruth

genealogy.note: A Moabitess (Ruth 1:4); no father or mother named. First married to Mahlon — Ruth 1:4 alone does not specify which brother she married; only Ruth 4:10 explicitly identifies her as "the wife of Mahlon." After Mahlon's death, married Boaz (Ruth 4:13). These marriages were sequential, not simultaneous.

verses.note: Named as one of the two Moabite women Naomi's sons married; the verse itself does not say which son married which wife.
Her vow of loyalty to Naomi: "whither thou goest, I will go... thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
Goes to glean; "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz."
Boaz commends her loyalty to Naomi and her leaving her own land to come to Israel.
Follows Naomi's instructions at the threshing floor and asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her, invoking his role as a near kinsman.
Boaz publicly takes her as wife (v.10); she conceives and bears a son (v.13).

funFacts: Ruth 4:10 is the only verse that specifies Mahlon (rather than Chilion) as her first husband — nothing earlier in the book states this directly.
She is one of only a few women in the Old Testament to have an entire book named after her.

characters.name: Boaz

genealogy.note: "Salmon begat Boaz" (Ruth 4:21) — stated directly within Ruth itself. Ruth never names Boaz's mother; do not treat the Matthew 1:5 identification of Salmon's wife as "Rachab" as part of this book's own claim (see funFacts hedge). Described as "a mighty man of wealth, of the family of Elimelech" (Ruth 2:1) — a kinsman of Elimelech, exact degree of relation not specified beyond that.

verses.note: Introduced as "a mighty man of wealth, of the family of Elimelech."
Instructs his reapers to let Ruth glean freely among the sheaves and shows her deliberate kindness.
At the threshing floor, agrees in principle to act as kinsman but discloses there is a kinsman nearer than himself.
Goes to the city gate, calls the nearer kinsman aside, and gathers ten elders as witnesses.
Publicly declares the land purchase and his marriage to Ruth before the witnesses.
Takes Ruth as wife; she bears Obed. Genealogy: "Salmon begat Boaz."

funFacts: Called "a mighty man of wealth" (Ruth 2:1) — the Hebrew phrase used elsewhere for military valor, here applied to a landowner/civic figure.

NAMING COLLISION FLAG: "Boaz" is also the name given to one of the two bronze pillars at the entrance of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:21; 2 Chronicles 3:17) — an object, not a person, but the identical name.

Matthew 1:5, a different book, names Salmon's wife as "Rachab" in its own genealogy of Christ — Ruth itself never names Boaz's mother, so that identification is noted here only as an external cross-reference, not asserted as this book's own claim.

characters.name: The Nearer Kinsman (unnamed)

genealogy.note: Deliberately left unnamed by the text — Boaz addresses him only as "Ho, such a one!" (Ruth 4:1). Described as a kinsman closer in relation to Elimelech's family than Boaz (Ruth 3:12, 4:3-4); the exact nature of that closer relation is not specified.

verses.note: Boaz tells Ruth, "it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I."
Boaz calls him to the gate: "Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here."
Boaz offers him the first right to redeem the parcel of land that was Elimelech's.
He declines: "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance: redeem thou my right to thyself; for I cannot redeem it."
The shoe-removal custom is performed to confirm the transfer of the redemption right to Boaz.

funFacts: The text withholds his name entirely, even while naming Elimelech, Naomi, Mahlon, Chilion, Ruth, Orpah, and Boaz — a deliberate narrative choice, not a textual gap.

His refusal (Ruth 4:6) is what legally clears the way for Boaz to redeem the land and marry Ruth — removing him from the story would change the outcome entirely, which is why he holds his own tier rather than being folded into Boaz's.

characters.name: The Line to David
characters.purpose: Closes the book by tracing descent from Judah's son Pharez (cf. Genesis 38) down through Boaz and Obed to Jesse and David, reframing the preceding story — and Ruth's Moabite origin within it — as directly ancestral to Israel's monarchy. (Attribution: Unattributed narrator's genealogical appendix (Ruth 4:18-22) — not spoken by any character in the story.)

verses.note: "Now these are the generations of Pharez: Pharez begat Hezron... and Jesse begat David." Ten links: Pharez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David.

funFacts: This is the only place in Ruth that names David outright, tying the whole preceding narrative to him as its endpoint.
Pharez is a figure from Genesis 38 (Judah and Tamar); Ruth's genealogy assumes that background without retelling it.

characters.name: Mahlon

genealogy.note: One of Naomi and Elimelech's two sons (Ruth 1:2). Identified specifically as Ruth's husband only in Ruth 4:10 — nothing earlier names which brother married which wife.

verses.note: Named as one of Elimelech and Naomi's two sons, Ephrathites of Bethlehemjudah.
"Mahlon and Chilion died also both of them" in Moab, leaving Naomi without husband or sons.

CORRECTION/HEDGE: Boaz's declaration names him specifically: "Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off." This name-raising clause follows directly from naming Ruth as Mahlon's wife. But the immediately preceding v.9 describes the purchased land as belonging jointly to "Elimelech's, and...Chilion's and Mahlon's" — the text does not fully separate whose specific "inheritance" is in view in v.10, and this entry does not assert a single flat resolution between the land-redemption (tied to the whole family estate) and the name-raising (tied to Mahlon by name).

funFacts: Ruth 4:10 is the only verse that specifies Mahlon, not Chilion, as Ruth's husband.
He has no quoted line and no individually differentiated action beyond marrying and dying (Ruth 1:4-5) — everything else attributed to him comes from the chapter 4 legal declaration after his death.

characters.name: Chilion

genealogy.note: One of Naomi and Elimelech's two sons (Ruth 1:2). HEDGE: the text never directly states Chilion married Orpah — Ruth 1:4 names Orpah and Ruth as the two daughters-in-law without pairing them to a specific son; Orpah is inferred as his wife only by elimination once Ruth 4:10 identifies Ruth specifically as Mahlon's wife. This pairing is not asserted as flat textual fact.

verses.note: Named as Elimelech and Naomi's other son.
Died in Moab along with Mahlon.
The land purchased by Boaz is described as including "all that was...Chilion's," alongside Elimelech's and Mahlon's.

funFacts: Unlike Mahlon, Chilion is never individually distinguished after Ruth 1:5 — no verse quotes him or singles out an action of his apart from his brother's.
No verse ever directly pairs him with Orpah by name — that pairing is inference by elimination only.

characters.name: Orpah
characters.perkNote: Departs the story rather than continuing to support Naomi — incidental to the ongoing arc, fits cost-cutter rather than loyalty-boost.

genealogy.note: A Moabitess, daughter-in-law of Naomi (Ruth 1:4). HEDGE: her marriage to Chilion specifically is inferred only by elimination from Ruth 4:10 (which names Ruth as Mahlon's wife), not stated directly anywhere in the text.

verses.note: Named as one of the two Moabite women who married Naomi's sons.
"And Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her" — she returns toward Moab after Naomi's urging.

funFacts: Her decision to return to Moab (Ruth 1:14-15) is not presented with any negative judgment in the text — Naomi explicitly urges both daughters-in-law to go back (Ruth 1:8-13), and Orpah simply takes the path Naomi herself offered.
She never reappears after Ruth 1:14.

characters.name: Boaz's Servant (unnamed overseer of the reapers)
characters.perkNote: Direct employee/supporter of Boaz — boosts Boaz's tier.

genealogy.note: Unnamed; described only as "his servant that was set over the reapers" (Ruth 2:5-6).

verses.note: Boaz asks him whose damsel Ruth is; he answers, identifying her as "the Moabitish damsel that came back with Naomi out of the country of Moab."
Reports her diligence: she asked to glean and has continued from the morning, with only a little rest.

funFacts: He is the first person in the book to describe Ruth's diligence to a third party, directly prompting Boaz's attention to her.
Left unnamed, like the nearer kinsman later in the book — the text names its core figures but leaves several supporting roles anonymous.

characters.name: Obed
characters.perkNote: Attached to Naomi because Ruth 4:14-17 frames his birth almost entirely around her ("There is a son born to Naomi"), even though he is Boaz and Ruth's biological son — see genealogy note.

genealogy.note: Biological son of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:13, 4:21). HEDGE: the text nonetheless frames his birth around Naomi — "There is a son born to Naomi" (Ruth 4:17) — and around raising up the name/inheritance connected to Ruth's late husband (Ruth 4:10). Naomi nurses him (Ruth 4:16). Grandfather of David through his son Jesse (Ruth 4:17, 22).

verses.note: Ruth conceives and bears a son, with Boaz as father.

The neighbor women bless Naomi, saying the child "shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age: for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him."
"And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it."
The neighbor women name him: "There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David."
Genealogy: "Obed begat Jesse, and Jesse begat David."

funFacts: His name is given by the neighbor women (Ruth 4:17), not by his parents Boaz or Ruth directly.

NAMING COLLISION FLAG: "Obed" is a repeated Old Testament name for several distinct people elsewhere — e.g. an unrelated Obed in the Jerahmeelite genealogy (1 Chronicles 2:37-38), an Obed among David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:47), and an Obed who was Azariah's father (2 Chronicles 23:1). None of these are this Obed.

genealogyLists.davidic_lineage_link_names_ruth_4_18-21: Pharez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, and Nahshon (Ruth 4:18-21) are named only within the closing genealogy, with no individual narrative action inside Ruth itself. Pharez is elsewhere identified in Genesis 38 as the son of Judah and Tamar, but Ruth itself does not restate that background. Salmon (4:20-21) is likewise only named in the genealogy, with a full note under his own naming-collision flag below.
genealogyLists.elders_and_witnesses_ruth_4_2_4_9-11: Ten elders of the city (Ruth 4:2) plus "all the people that were in the gate" (Ruth 4:11) serve as witnesses to Boaz's redemption of the land and marriage to Ruth, and jointly bless the marriage. None are individually named or differentiated.
genealogyLists.women_neighbours_ruth_4_14-17: Unnamed women, described as Naomi's neighbours, bless her at Obed's birth (Ruth 4:14-15) and are the ones who collectively give the child his name, "Obed" (Ruth 4:17). A single undifferentiated collective act; no individuals are named.
genealogyLists.jesse_and_david_ruth_4_17_22: Jesse and David are named only as the final two links of the closing genealogy (Ruth 4:17, 22) — Obed's son and grandson respectively — with no narrative action of their own inside Ruth itself; the book ends at the moment their names appear.
genealogyLists.naming_collision_flags_hezron_ram_ammina: HEZRON: a second, unrelated Hezron (son of Reuben, Genesis 46:9; Exodus 6:14) is distinct from the Hezron of Ruth 4:18-19 (son of Pharez, of the tribe of Judah). RAM: 1 Chronicles 2:25,27 names a different Ram as firstborn of Jerahmeel, Hezron's other son-line — distinct from the Ram of Ruth 4:19 (son of Hezron via the Pharez line, ancestor of Boaz); Job 32:2's "kindred of Ram" (Elihu the Buzite) is also likely unrelated. AMMINADAB: a separate Levite/Kohathite Amminadab appears in 1 Chronicles 6:22 and 15:10-11, distinct from the Amminadab of Ruth 4:19-20 (father of Nahshon, of Judah) — though this Judahite Amminadab is likely the same one named as Elisheba's father in Exodus 6:23, since Nahshon is named there as her brother, matching the same family line. SALMON: near-collision only, not a true name clash — "Salmon" the person (Ruth 4:20-21, Boaz's father) is unrelated to Mount Salmon/Zalmon, a place name in Judges 9:48 and Psalm 68:14.

1. FLAGGED ISSUE ADDRESSED: the first draft attributed the "raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" language (Ruth 4:9-10) to Elimelech as flat fact. This redraft hedges explicitly in BOTH the elimelech and mahlon entries: Ruth 4:9 describes the land purchase as covering the joint estate of "Elimelech's, and...Chilion's and Mahlon's," while Ruth 4:10 ties the specific name-raising clause to Mahlon by name as Ruth's husband. Neither entry asserts a single flat resolution of which "inheritance" v.10 refers to; the overlap/ambiguity is called out in both places rather than assigned as settled fact to either man alone.

2. NAMING COLLISIONS FLAGGED (per the mandatory re-scan): Boaz (also names one of Solomon's temple pillars, 1 Kings 7:21/2 Chronicles 3:17); Obed (at least three other biblical Obeds — 1 Chronicles 2:37-38, 1 Chronicles 11:47, 2 Chronicles 23:1); Hezron (a second, unrelated Hezron son of Reuben in Genesis 46:9/Exodus 6:14); Ram (a second Ram, son of Jerahmeel, in 1 Chronicles 2:25); Amminadab (a distinct Levite Amminadab in 1 Chronicles 6:22/15:10-11, though the Judahite Amminadab here is likely the same one named in Exodus 6:23 via the shared figure Nahshon); Salmon (near-collision only, with the place name Mount Salmon/Zalmon, Judges 9:48/Psalm 68:14). Full detail logged in genealogyLists.naming_collision_flags_hezron_ram_amminadab_salmon. No collision found worth flagging for Elimelech, Naomi, Ruth, Mahlon, Chilion, or Orpah.

3. UNRESOLVED-BY-DESIGN AMBIGUITIES HEDGED, NOT INVENTED: (a) which brother, Mahlon or Chilion, married which wife is never stated outright in Ruth 1:4 — only Ruth 4:10 disambiguates Mahlon/Ruth, leaving Chilion/Orpah as inference by elimination, flagged in both chilion and orpah entries; (b) Boaz's mother is not named anywhere in Ruth itself — the traditional/Matthew 1:5 identification with Rahab is noted only as an external cross-reference in Boaz's funFacts, not asserted as part of this book's own genealogy data, per the rule that a later-scripture name may only be used when THIS book's own text links the two mentions (it does not); (c) Obed's submanager attachment to Naomi (rather than to his biological parents Boaz/Ruth) is flagged in his own perkNote/genealogy.note as a deliberate, textually-grounded but non-exclusive choice, since Ruth 4:14-17 frames his birth almost entirely around Naomi's restoration.

All five parentManagerId values (mahlon→elimelech, chilion→elimelech, orpah→naomi, boaz_servant→boaz, obed→naomi) resolve to a matching characters[] entry, each held by an actual tier-holding manager. No character holds both a scribeTier and a parentManagerId. Bulk/undifferentiated groups (the ten elders and witnesses, the neighbour women, and the bare lineage names Pharez/Hezron/Ram/Amminadab/Nahshon/Jesse/David) were kept out of characters[] and placed in genealogyLists per methodology point 8, since none of them have an individually differentiated action or quoted line distinct from the group.

5. TIER COUNT: five person tiers (Elimelech, Naomi, Ruth, Boaz, the Nearer Kinsman) plus one law/theme tier (the closing Line to David genealogy) — scaled to Ruth's genuinely small, intimate cast per methodology point 1, not padded to match larger books' tier counts.
